title: Equi Join
description: Match explicit equality roles across relations, preserve complete composite identities, and distinguish predicate form from output projection, duplicate elimination and outer preservation.
notes:
## Equality identifies the qualifying combinations

An equi join uses equality comparisons for its matching predicate. Employee.department_id equals Department.department_id is a familiar example. The column names need not be identical, because the predicate explicitly states which roles are compared. The condition connects values according to the modeled relationship rather than assuming that every same-named column is a suitable match.

In the classical inner-join account, an equi join is a theta join restricted to equality comparisons. It returns qualifying matched tuple combinations. A predicate that combines equality with a greater-than condition is not purely equality-based under this terminology. The classification describes the predicate form, not every other semantic property of a complete SQL query.

## Attribute meaning matters beyond equal values

Two integer attributes can share a value without representing the same identity domain. Employee.department_id is meaningful to compare with the department key in the stated model, but an employee identifier equal to a course credit amount does not establish a useful relationship. SQL type compatibility and a TRUE comparison do not prove the domain connection was intended.

Use declared identities, documented references, and the actual application contract to choose the comparison. Descriptive names can repeat or change, so joining on a label can misassociate facts even if a small fixture looks correct. Two employees named Asha remain distinct through their identifiers, and two departments can share a descriptive label under a model permitting that repetition.

## Inner matching and output projection are separate

A SELECT star over an explicit ON equality join generally exposes columns from both sources, including both compared roles. If Employee.department_id equals Department.id, the output can include both values even though they agree in a matched row. The equality predicate does not automatically remove one column or deduplicate every source attribute.

An explicit projection can keep just the needed roles and label them clearly. USING or NATURAL forms can have different merged-column output conventions in supported SQL syntax. Do not claim only a natural join can omit a redundant displayed comparison column; an ordinary explicit SELECT list can do so while preserving a precise predicate. Matching semantics and result shape need separate explanations.

## One parent can match many children

Suppose Department 7 has two employees. An inner join from Employee to Department produces two combinations, one per matching employee. The repeated department label is correct at that result grain. It does not mean the department entity was stored twice or that the query should automatically apply DISTINCT to every displayed field.

If both compared inputs allow repeated matching values, the join can produce several combinations per value. Two rows on one side and three on the other can yield six matches. An equality condition does not imply one-to-one cardinality. Keys, uniqueness constraints, source population, and additional predicates determine the actual maximums and observed multiplicity.

## Multi-column equality preserves scoped identity

A room can be identified by building_id together with room_number. A booking intended for Building 7 Room 101 should compare both components to Room. Joining only room_number can match Building 9 Room 101 as well, producing an incorrect capacity or duplicated booking output. Both identifiers can be required even though the predicate remains an equi join.

```sql
SELECT b.booking_id, r.building_id, r.room_number, r.capacity
FROM bookings b
JOIN rooms r
  ON r.building_id = b.building_id
 AND r.room_number = b.room_number
ORDER BY b.booking_id;
```

The combined equality follows the complete intended identity. It does not enforce native booking references merely by reading matching records. An inner query can omit unsupported proposals rather than reject their insertion. Native foreign-key operations and accepted application writes require evidence at their own enforcement boundary.

## Missing values affect ordinary equality

In SQL, an ordinary equality involving NULL yields UNKNOWN rather than a TRUE match. An optional department reference with no assignment therefore produces no matched inner department row through that predicate. A preserving join can retain the employee with missing partner output if the report requires all employees, but preservation is a separate feature from the equality form.

A NULL-safe comparison can implement a different explicit value-matching contract on the supported engine. It should not be introduced casually for identity references, because two absent identifiers do not automatically denote one real entity. State whether the task compares actual required identities, optional data values, or result tuples with specified set-operation absence handling.

## Outer joins can also use equality predicates

A left outer join can use Employee.department_id equals Department.id while preserving unmatched employees. This has an equality-based ON condition, but it includes null-extended unmatched results beyond a classical inner equi join. Use precise wording when the term equi describes the predicate while another term describes preservation behaviour.

This distinction prevents a misleading shortcut that every equality join behaves like an inner join or that every outer join is merely product followed by selection. The ON predicate determines matches; the selected join type determines whether and how unmatched input occurrences survive. A report with a root, optional reference, or invalid staging value can expose that difference.

## Explicit conditions are stable against unrelated names

Natural joins choose comparisons from common attribute names, which can make them sensitive to schema changes. An explicit equi predicate states the intended roles even when their names differ. Adding an unrelated same-named attribute does not silently add a new comparison to the explicit ON condition. That can make the data contract easier to review and maintain.

The explicit predicate can still be wrong, so clarity is not a substitute for correctness. A copied ON expression comparing the wrong id can return plausible matches if numeric values overlap. Review nearest callers, definitions, and representative tuples before assuming an explicit-looking statement follows the intended relationship. The exercise's fixture uses meaningful role names to make the choice observable.

## Filtering changes the joined population

A report may need only active employees or only departments in a given scope. Those conditions affect which combinations qualify for the final result. In an inner query, several equivalent formulations can preserve the intended matched set under their assumptions. In an outer query, moving a condition between ON and WHERE can change preservation and must be reviewed deliberately.

A department label filter placed in WHERE after a left join can reject unmatched employees, even when the FROM clause says LEFT JOIN. The full statement determines the returned population. The equality condition alone does not prove that every parent or child remains in the result. State the required inclusion of unmatched occurrences before selecting syntax.

## Counts need the intended identity grain

Counting matched employee-department combinations can equal employee count when each employee has one valid matching department, but it does not automatically equal distinct department count. A grouped department report needs to count the desired child identity and preserve empty departments if required. DISTINCT over a numeric amount or name is not generally a substitute for counting entity identities.

For room bookings, several bookings can validly reference the same room. That repetition belongs to the booking population. A pair listing should retain booking_id when separate bookings matter. Removing it and deduplicating room labels changes the question to which rooms are represented, potentially losing legitimate separate occurrences that need different handling.

## Logical matching does not choose the physical strategy

Equality predicates can support useful indexes or join algorithms, but the available engine, data, statistics, and full query determine execution. An equi join is not automatically fast, one-to-one, or foreign-key-enforced. A local result fixture verifies semantics rather than large-scale cost. Use actual supported plan and runtime evidence if performance is part of the requirement.

Likewise, a query does not grant permission to read employee or booking details. The application needs trusted access controls at its actual boundary. Matching an existing identity is different from deciding who may view or mutate that fact. The synthetic exercises make no production authorization claim even when the tables resemble common application structures.

## Verify explicit roles and complete identities

Use several employees in one department, repeated names, an unmatched optional reference, the same room number under different owners, and several bookings for one room. Check that output preserves the stated occurrence grain and that incomplete comparison components do not create extra matches. An empty partner population should produce no matched inner rows under the exercise contract.

The exercises verify explicit employee-department matching and complete composite room references on isolated SQL fixtures. They distinguish predicate form, projection, duplicate multiplicity, and unmatched-row handling while keeping native enforcement and exact MySQL/provider gaps separate. Equi joins are useful when equality connects the right semantic roles and every identity component is retained, allowing readable combinations without assuming that equal types, common names, or successful execution prove the whole relationship contract.

questions.question_text: What makes a join specifically an Equi Join?
options: It always involves exactly two tables
Its join condition uses ONLY equality (=) comparisons
It never returns duplicate column names
It requires the ON clause to be omitted
questions.explanation: Equi Join is precisely the equality-restricted special case of Theta Join.

questions.question_text: In the illustrated explicit ON inner equi join with SELECT *, are both compared source columns available in the output?
options: No, duplicate-valued columns are automatically merged
Yes — an Equi Join's result keeps both matched columns from each side, even though their values are identical for matched rows
Only department_id appears in the result
This causes an error
questions.explanation: The explicit ON equality does not merge columns. Projection and supported USING/NATURAL output conventions can produce other shapes.

questions.question_text: Is `ON a.x = b.x AND a.y > b.y` a pure Equi Join?
options: Yes, since it contains an equality comparison
No — since it mixes an equality with a non-equality comparison, the overall condition makes this a (non-equi) Theta Join
This is a Natural Join
This is an invalid join condition
questions.explanation: 'Equi Join' specifically requires EVERY comparison in the condition to be equality; mixing in a non-equality comparison makes it a general Theta Join.

questions.question_text: Can an Equi Join match on multiple column pairs at once?
options: No, only a single equality comparison is ever allowed
Yes — multiple equality comparisons can be combined with AND, and it remains an Equi Join as long as all comparisons are equality
Multiple column pairs would make it a Cartesian Product instead
This would require a Theta Join instead
questions.explanation: A composite-key style match using several equality comparisons combined with AND is still a valid Equi Join.

questions.question_text: Why might Equi Join be preferred over Natural Join when the matching columns have different names?
options: Equi Join cannot handle differently-named columns either
Equi Join lets you explicitly specify which columns to equate regardless of their names, while Natural Join specifically requires matching column NAMES
Natural Join is always faster regardless of column names
There is no meaningful difference between them
questions.explanation: Equi Join's explicit ON condition works regardless of column naming; Natural Join's automatic matching depends on identical names.

questions.question_text: Is Equi Join a special case of Theta Join, or a completely separate concept?
options: A completely separate, unrelated concept
A special case — Equi Join is exactly a Theta Join whose condition is restricted to equality only
Theta Join is a special case of Equi Join instead
They are exact synonyms with no distinction at all
questions.explanation: Equi Join narrows Theta Join's general 'any comparison' condition down to equality specifically.

questions.question_text: Which is a common appropriate equi-join task when the modeled reference is valid?
options: Comparing date ranges between two tables
Matching a foreign key in one table to the primary key it references in another table
Finding rows with the maximum value in a column
Sorting a table's rows
questions.explanation: An explicit foreign-key-to-parent-key comparison is common, but an arbitrary equality query does not itself prove native reference enforcement.

questions.question_text: How can an explicit ON equi join omit one redundant displayed comparison column without changing its matching predicate?
options: Theta Join
Use an explicit SELECT list; supported NATURAL or USING forms also have their own merged-column conventions
Cartesian Product
Outer Join
questions.explanation: Natural join is not the only way to avoid displaying both compared columns. Matching and selected output roles are different concerns.

questions.question_text: Does an equality predicate imply one-to-one matching?
options: Yes; every equality is a key
No; repeated values can create many combinations
Only if columns have different names
Only if names repeat
questions.explanation: Uniqueness and source populations determine multiplicity.

questions.question_text: Can equality compare differently named columns?
options: No; names must match
Only NATURAL can join different names
Yes, when the explicit roles and domains are appropriate
Only if both tables are empty
questions.explanation: The ON expression identifies the intended comparison.

questions.question_text: Why compare building_id and room_number together for a booking?
options: Only capacity identifies the room
Every room number is globally unique
The room identity is scoped to its building
The query will infer missing components
questions.explanation: A partial comparison can match another owner’s room.

questions.question_text: What happens to NULL under ordinary equality?
options: It always equals zero
It matches every missing parent as a real entity
It becomes an empty string
The comparison is UNKNOWN rather than a TRUE match
questions.explanation: Absence handling must be part of the SQL contract.

questions.question_text: Can a left outer join use an equality ON predicate?
options: Yes; predicate form and unmatched-row preservation are different dimensions
No; all equality joins are inner
Only if it has no columns
Only if one side is empty
questions.explanation: The complete join type determines preservation.

questions.question_text: Does selecting one of two matched id columns change the ON predicate?
options: Yes; it deletes the relationship
No; projection chooses output roles
Only if aliases are used
Only if columns are numeric
questions.explanation: Result shape and matching semantics differ.

questions.question_text: What can a new unrelated common column change in a NATURAL join but not an unchanged explicit ON condition?
options: Every primary key value
The stored user permissions
The set of implicit equality comparisons
The number of databases
questions.explanation: Explicit predicates avoid that particular name-based coupling.

questions.question_text: Why can joining on employee_name be unsafe?
options: Names cannot be text
Every label is a foreign key
Ids never repeat across roles
Different employee identities can share a name
questions.explanation: Descriptive coincidence is not a reliable identity rule.

questions.question_text: Two occurrences match three occurrences on the other side. How many pairs can an equality join produce?
options: 1 always
2 always
3 always
questions.explanation: Bag-like occurrence combinations can multiply.

questions.question_text: Does an inner matching query reject unsupported reference proposals at insert time?
options: Yes; JOIN creates a foreign key
No; a query can simply omit unmatched records
Only if ORDER BY appears
Only if output is empty
questions.explanation: Read semantics and trusted write enforcement differ.

questions.question_text: What can a WHERE predicate on a nullable right side do after LEFT JOIN?
options: Always preserve every left row
Change every equality to NULL-safe equality
Reject unmatched preserved rows depending on the predicate
Automatically create a parent
questions.explanation: The whole query determines the returned population.

questions.question_text: What does a local equi-join fixture not prove?
options: The exercised fixture matches
The tested output labels
The explicit result sequence
Production authority, native constraint enforcement or runtime performance at scale
questions.explanation: Verification claims must stay within the executed scope.

coding_problems.title: Match employee assignments through the explicit department identity
coding_problems.task: Return employee_id, employee_name and department_name for employees with a matching department. Keep separate employees sharing a name. Unassigned or invalid references do not contribute inner matches.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE departments (department_id INT PRIMARY KEY, department_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id INT PRIMARY KEY, employee_name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL, department_id INT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO departments VALUES (7,'Computing'),(9,'History'); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'Asha',7),(2,'Asha',7),(3,'Mira',NULL),(4,'Dev',99);
coding_problems.expected:
employee_id	employee_name	department_name
1	Asha	Computing
2	Asha	Computing
constraints: Staging intentionally permits invalid references to make inner-match scope explicit; no native FK is declared.
edge_cases: One department can match several employees.
Missing and unmatched assignments do not invent partner rows.
hints: Use explicit equality between the modeled department identifiers.
Project the requested source roles rather than every available column.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT e.employee_id, e.employee_name, d.department_name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id ORDER BY e.employee_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The explicit predicate follows the intended identity relationship while the projection determines the displayed fields.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO departments VALUES (7,'Computing'); INSERT INTO employees VALUES (9,'Mira',7);

coding_problems.title: Match complete building-room identities for booking facts
coding_problems.task: Return booking_id, building_id, room_number and capacity for each booking matching a complete room identity. Do not match the same local number in another building.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE rooms (building_id INT NOT NULL, room_number INT NOT NULL, capacity INT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(building_id,room_number));
CREATE TABLE bookings (booking_id INT PRIMARY KEY, building_id INT NOT NULL, room_number INT NOT NULL);
constraints: Every room identity includes its owner.
The fixture is a query mirror, not native booking-reference or production authority verification.
edge_cases: Several bookings can refer to one room.
A matching partial discriminator under another owner is insufficient.
hints: Combine both equality comparisons with AND.
Keep booking_id to preserve the requested occurrence grain.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT b.booking_id, r.building_id, r.room_number, r.capacity FROM bookings b JOIN rooms r ON r.building_id = b.building_id AND r.room_number = b.room_number ORDER BY b.booking_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The complete equi predicate prevents owner confusion while preserving separate booking facts and selected room properties.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO rooms VALUES (9,101,40); INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (1,7,101);
INSERT INTO rooms VALUES (7,101,30); INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (2,7,101),(1,7,101);
